#7386. I Blind-Tested 3 Gemini Models On Real SEO Questions – Neon Won 5 Of 6 via @sejournal, @marie_haynes

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Is the newest AI model actually better, or do we just assume it is? My blind test of three Gemini models gave a clear answer.

Over the last few months, I have been quietly building something I call Marie’s Brain – a private AI co-pilot grounded in my hand-curated Open Knowledge Format (OKF) library of Search and AI research.

Recently, I switched the tool over to Google’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. After using it for a while, though, I had a nagging feeling: Is Hydrogen actually producing better answers than Gemini 3.8 Flash, or am I just assuming newer means better?

Instead of guessing, I decided to run a real blind taste test – and threw Gemini 4 Neon into the mix too.

You can actually try the exact same six-question blind test yourself here (columns A, B, and C are shuffled on every question, and there is a button at the top to reveal how I voted and the real token costs).

The blind 3-way taste test interface: columns A, B, and C are shuffled on every SEO question, complete with clickable OKF concept pills. Try voting blind yourself here. Image Credit: Marie Haynes

Before I even finished reading the first round of blind outputs, one thing jumped out immediately: The answers were way too long.

My Brain had been defaulting to Detailed mode with no word ceiling. When we checked the API logs, we discovered something wild: Gemini 4 Hydrogen was going into an over-eager research loop, reading an average of 21 OKF files per question, taking 68 seconds, writing 1,600-word essays, and costing $0.44 per prompt – actually more expensive per turn than Gemini 4 Neon!

On top of that, some answers were dropping internal Google engineering jargon (like MAGIT and FastSearch) that a busy business owner does not need to wade through just to figure out why their clicks dropped.

So before doing my real blind vote, I made three quick upgrades to how Marie’s Brain works:

Then we re-ran the exact same six real-world SEO and AI Search questions – covering AI Overviews and traffic drops, whether to delete or rewrite informational posts, Main Content on commercial buyer’s guides, pruning thin location pages, agent readiness and /llms.txt, and a realistic five-hour-a-week plan that skips GEO distractions – across Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 4 Hydrogen, and Gemini 4 Neon.

With the model names hidden and the columns randomized, I read all 18 answers and picked a winner on every prompt.

When I hit reveal, the result wasn’t even close:

What stood out to me about Neon wasn’t that it had more facts – all three models pulled from the exact same OKF files. It was how it communicated. Neon’s answers felt more like a smart human thinking through a problem rather than a predictable AI response. I genuinely enjoyed reading them, and I immediately understood what they were trying to get across.

My revealed blind test results (5/6 for Gemini 4 Neon), real Gemini API token usage, and pace-adjusted monthly cost estimates per user. Image Credit: Marie Haynes

Of course, better answers only matter if the economics make sense. Here are the real numbers from our live Concise-mode runs (using real Gemini API usageMetadata, including thinking tokens, at conservative uncached list rates):

Note on Neon’s speed: That 70.8s average was skewed by one single 3.5-minute API queue spike during testing; typical Neon replies ran 18 to 40 seconds (with text streaming on screen as it writes).

At first glance, $191 vs. $93 per 1,000 prompts sounds like a big jump (about 10 cents extra per prompt). But when I mapped that against realistic full-month usage paces extrapolated from my early active users, here is what the extra cost per user looks like:

And those are conservative uncached estimates. Because every turn references the same ~55,000-token OKF Master Index, Gemini 4 Neon’s implicit context caching discounts repeated input tokens across multi-turn chats, bringing real-world bills noticeably lower.

I like learning about Google. I’ve been obsessively learning and sharing everything I can about how Search works since 2008. ...

#7383. Reddit’s AEO Tool Recommendations Have A Promoter Problem via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

An analysis of subreddits flagged most users weighing in on AEO tools as likely promoters. Among the rest, accuracy was the top feature complaint.

Graphite flagged 55% of the users who gave an opinion of an AEO tool across 54 subreddits this year as likely working for or promoting a marketing software product.

Among the users it didn’t flag, the accuracy of visibility scores drew more unfavorable opinions than any other product feature.

The growth agency picked subreddits where AEO comes up regularly and found 5,990 posts and 25,392 comments from January through September that mention a tool. OpenAI language models labeled the mentions, the opinions and the likely promoters.

The agency helps companies with AEO and SEO and says it doesn’t sell AEO tools or accept payment to be mentioned. Its CEO, Ethan Smith, is an investor in Peec AI, one of three tools tied for the highest score in the analysis.

Graphite flagged 1,298 of the 2,365 Reddit users who gave an opinion of an AEO tool or a marketing platform’s AEO features.

A user was flagged when the agency’s model put the chance at 50% or more that their posts promoted a marketing product they build, own, work for, sell or partner with. That includes SEO, AEO, sales and web analytics tools. An agency’s description of its own client work did not constitute promotion.

To test the model, the company manually inspected 43 of the users it had flagged. Ultimately, 12% of them disclosed being promoters, while 62% were found to have promoted a product but failed to identify themselves as such; the remaining ones were judged non-promoters. The write-up also says that some of the models’ labeling decisions could be incorrect.

Four types of likely promoter Reddit accounts were identified. Each type exhibited a pattern across several posts or comments.

One account was used to recommend the same lesser-known tracking service on eight posts and comments. In January this user claimed that they switched from a competitor, and 11 days later they commented about possibly purchasing the product.

Another account made reference to a little-known product in four comments with well-known tracking services over the course of eight days.

A third account posted three separate times for the same product within 12 minutes.

Over six weeks, 38 accounts recommended the same product in 52 comments, each using the phrase “from what I’ve read” in its recommendation. That phrase appears with any other tool no more than twice.

Of the opinions regarding the accuracy of AEO tools from users who weren’t flagged, 143 were negative while 27 had positive views. No other feature elicited as many negative opinions. These users provided opinions on 44 tools, for a total of 1,557 opinions.

Graphite’s chart compares praise and criticism across features after excluding opinions from users it flagged as likely promoters.

According to the write-up, users frequently view visibility scores as estimates due to variation in AI answers among different runs, locations and users. Several have advised fellow users to “treat them as trend, not truth” and to verify the information through manual review.

The citation data, or the citations used by AI systems as source material for their answers, was generally viewed positively by users. Price received more user opinions than any other attribute and most of those opinions were negative, at 182 negative versus 98 positive.

The agency also evaluated the 11 tools which generated sufficient opinions using a 0-100 point scale; a score of 50 represented neutral. Each of the 11 tools scored between 54 and 66 points. The authors also said the ranges around many of the tools’ scores overlapped and therefore, the differences in scores could lack statistical significance.

Graphite’s count puts a number on how many Reddit users weighing in on AEO tools may be promoting marketing software. Before a tool recommended on Reddit goes on your shortlist, check the account’s history for repeat plugs and a story that changes from post to post.

Graphite’s tool scores reflect opinions from January through September, and the company says their order could change as more opinions come in. Complaints about the accuracy of visibility scores give you something to test before renewing. Run a sample of your tracked prompts by hand and compare the results with the tool’s numbers.

Featured Image: Accogliente Design/Shutterstock

#7382. TikTok adds new AI transparency and parental controls

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The platform announced a range of updates at its third Safety and Innovation Summit, including new ways to protect creators and teens.

TikTok announced a range of updates at its third Safety and Innovation Summit last week, including a new tool that helps users identify artificial intelligence-generated content, a likeness detection feature to protect creator IP and new tools and resources for parents and schools.

First, TikTok announced a new AI transparency tool that will enable users to check if an image or video has been created using its AI tools.

As explained by TikTok: “People can upload an image or video to see whether it was generated or edited with TikTok’s AI creation features, even if they don’t have a TikTok account.”

The process will check the image or video for signs of TikTok’s digital watermarking on AI-generated content, providing another means to verify content in the app. That could also help to stop the spread of misinformation and harmful content.

TikTok said the tool is now available via its Transparency Center.

TikTok also announced a likeness detection tool that enables creators to verify their likeness, which will then facilitate image cross-matching against incoming uploads.

TikTok said creators will verify their ID with a trusted third-party partner, which will empower the system to detect and raise awareness of content that includes their image.

“They can report content directly to our safety teams,” the company said. “Content that violates our community guidelines against harmful, misleading or nonconsensual depiction of private individuals will be removed.”

The tool is now available to eligible creators and public figures.

TikTok also announced updates to its Family Pairing process, in order to give parents more visibility into how their teens are using the app and who they’re connecting with.

TikTok's updated Family Pairing also now includes more data on what kids are posting, as well as a new element that will enable parents to see what their kids are being shown in the app.

As explained by TikTok: “Parents can watch a sample of content from verified creators their teen follows, providing a snapshot of the communities and topic areas shaping their experience. More than 80% of parents of teens that we spoke to told us they want this kind of feature.”

TikTok also made its screen time element more prominent to help ensure that parents are aware of how much time their kids are spending in the app, and when in the day they’re active.

TikTok said it’s also working with leading experts to build a new alert for parents, which will let them know if their teen makes repeated searches for known terms related to self-harm.

“This notification will let them know that their teen may have tried to find potentially harmful content and provide thoughtful, expert-backed guidance on how to check in and start a conversation,” TikTok said.

Finally, TikTok launched a new Educator's Guide, which will provide teachers with additional resources to help advise teens on mindful social media usage behaviors.

These additional AI insight tools and the new parental experience controls should offer more ways for people to understand what’s happening in the app.

That could also provide more assurance for parents. And with more regions considering teen social media bans, additional understanding could also help TikTok reduce negative sentiment around the app.

#7381. Container Engineer at Supabase

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth. More than 9 million developers and 250,000+ customers now build on Supabase, and the majority of new databases on the platform are created by AI app builders — so the systems underneath have to stay reliable while they grow fast.

Container Engineering (ConEng) owns the internal container platform that runs Supabase's multi-tenant, multi-region services — the managed Kubernetes platform that other engineering teams build and deploy on top of. We own cluster lifecycle and cluster classes, multi-cluster and multi-region topology, capacity, scheduling, isolation and runtime safety, the higher-level platform APIs, the Kubernetes deployment contract and Argo semantics, rollout primitives, and runtime configuration and secret injection.

Your job is to make the platform itself trustworthy, observable, and cheap to operate at scale — and to raise the reliability bar for everyone who depends on it. This is not a gatekeeper role. You'll make the reliable path the easy path: building the automation and platform APIs that let product teams run safely by default, instrumenting what we operate, and making sure that when something breaks we detect it and recover fast.

Tooling & ecosystem — deep knowledge of the container and orchestration landscape (Kubernetes, containerd/OCI, the CNCF ecosystem) and a clear point of view on how to compose it.

Software engineering — designing and building the platform's automation, controllers, and internal tooling as production code, including solutions that don't come pre-shaped by an existing tool.

Operational / SRE practice — the discipline (SLOs, error budgets, incident response, ORRs) that runs the platform at scale as a predictable one.

We expect you to be genuinely deep in at least one of these, and many of our strongest candidates are deep in two (usually leaning toward one). Bringing real strength across all three is rare and exceptional — and even then, no one is equally strong in all three at once, so you'd focus where you're most needed at any given time. Different profiles are welcome here; tell us which of these is your center of gravity.

Regardless of the skill set, all team members carry a share of the team's on-call rota, responding to platform incidents and driving them to resolution and follow-up.

Define SLIs/SLOs and error budgets for the container platform itself, and build error-budget policies that actually gate platform changes.

Own the Operational Readiness Review (ORR) process for new platform capabilities and major changes.

Design and track metrics for platform uptime, and increase observability into the platform by capturing the right metrics, logs, and traces across the platform layers.

Drive the incident-to-improvement pipeline: facilitate blameless postmortems, connect findings to readiness gaps, spot repeat failure patterns, and push through systemic fixes.

Build and maintain the platform's automation, controllers, operators, and internal tooling — writing production code and shipping it, not just wiring together existing tools.

Design and implement the platform-side CI/CD and rollout primitives that speed up platform deployments while working within proper change and release management.

Implement and maintain security automation for the platform: intrusion detection, automated remediation, and patch management.

Identify and quantify operational toil, and build the automation that removes it rather than just documenting it.

Contribute to the platform's continual testing automation — the test suites and pipelines that validate platform releases are fit for purpose before they reach tenants.

Act as a platform reliability and architecture expert — contribute to failure-mode analysis, dependency mapping, and resilience design for multi-tenant container workloads.

Evaluate and evolve the platform's tooling ecosystem (orchestration, runtime, networking, isolation, and observability stack) with a clear, opinionated view on trade-offs.

Improve system architecture to reduce infrastructure cost while balancing security, reliability, and performance across tenants.

Guide teams building on the platform to design sustainable on-call practices for their own services: alert quality, escalation paths, runbook coverage, and noise reduction.

Have 5+ years in platform engineering, container/Kubernetes platform operations, SRE, or production infrastructure, and have operated production systems at scale and carried on-call for them.

Are genuinely deep in at least one — ideally two — of the three strength areas below (and tell us which is your center of gravity):

Tooling & ecosystem — know the container/orchestration landscape well: Kubernetes, containerd and the OCI/CRI standards, and the surrounding CNCF ecosystem (e.g. Argo CD/Argo Rollouts for GitOps and progressive delivery; Cilium/eBPF networking and the Gateway API; Karpenter/KEDA-style autoscaling; and workload-isolation runtimes such as gVisor or Kata Containers). You reason about trade-offs rather than reaching for defaults.

Software engineering — write real production code (Go and/or a comparable systems language) and can build controllers, operators, and platform APIs — stepping back to the underlying problem and building the right solution when no off-the-shelf tool fits.

Operational / SRE practice — are fluent in SLOs, error budgets, and operational KPIs; have led incident response and blameless postmortems; and have driven down MTTD/MTTR for systems you operated.

Have worked with large-scale multi-tenant systems and understand isolation as a spectrum — from namespaces, RBAC, network policies, and resource quotas through to stronger primitives such as virtual clusters (e.g. vCluster) or VM-class runtimes.

Operate confidently on AWS (multiple accounts, IAM, VPC) and are comfortable with infrastructure-as-code (Pulumi preferred; Terraform/CDK also fine) and Kubernetes.

Script and automate to eliminate toil rather than absorb it.

Communicate clearly with both infrastructure specialists and product engineers, and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and iterating toward better systems over time.

Experience building and operating a multi-tenant Kubernetes platform that internal teams deploy onto.

Familiarity with policy engines (Kyverno, or OPA/Gatekeeper) and cost-attribution tooling (OpenCost/Kubecost) for per-tenant chargeback/showback.

Experience with managed database platforms or Postgres.

Familiarity with OpenTelemetry, Prometheus/VictoriaMetrics, Grafana, or similar observability tooling.

#7379. YouTube adds co-view counts to CTV metrics

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The platform will now CTV view counts based on television industry standards, and apply those new view counts across formats moving forward.

YouTube will now report higher viewer counts on CTV, with the addition of co-views to its CTV stats. YouTube said that the expanded numbers will provide a more accurate reflection of total viewer numbers.

As per YouTube, CTV viewing has become a major part of the YouTube experience, with over a billion hours of YouTube content now being watched on TV sets every day. But videos watched via CTV are often viewed by several people sitting in front of a TV set together, and as such, YouTube’s current CTV view count metric approach is too limited, because it only shows a single viewer per CTV session. That’s why the company is updating how it counts CTV views.

The solution, however, is based on estimates, because YouTube can’t track actual CTV viewer counts.

YouTube announced the addition of co-views in May, when Rene Ritchie, the platform’s head of editorial, gave an overview of the logic behind how YouTube will calculate co-views.

At the time, Ritchie said that YouTube would add additional viewers to CTV views “based on factors like demographics, video genre, even time of day.”

In its most recent announcement, Ritchie provided more clarity, saying that co-views would provide a more complete picture, “aligning with TV industry standards, including how traditional broadcast and streaming networks estimate the total number of people exposed to content.”

So how does the TV industry estimate TV viewers?

Audience analytics company Nielsen uses a people meter with families who take part in its research panel, which sees different family members manually reporting their viewing behaviors via response buttons when they're watching. The rise of VOD services with individual log-ins has expanded the pool of information on this front, and based on these sources, YouTube appears to be using an industry-standard estimation measure to suggest total CTV viewers of each video, which will then be reflected in its view counts.

Which won’t be exact, of course, but it could be more accurate than the current system.

Ritchie added that historical view counts won't be changed, and that co-views will only be applied to new TV views, including new views of old videos.

Ritchie also said that co-views won't impact ad revenue or YPP thresholds, while, creator earnings, AdSense payouts and YouTube partner program eligibility will still be based on qualified views and watch hours.

Though the change will impact watch time metrics.

As per Ritchie “While co-views also don't impact metrics like thumbnail impressions, click-through rates and average view duration, watch time will be consistent with the updated public view counts to reflect the co-view audience watching together.”

In other words, watch time calculations will rise based on the assumption that more people are watching at certain times. So if YouTube estimated that three people were watching a video, for example, the watch time count for that video would then be tripled for that session.

The change will see many YouTube videos get higher view counts and watch time results, so if there’s a sudden spike in these metrics, this is likely why.

YouTube’s co-view update is being rolled out to all channels.

#7377. Instagram chief shares Muse tips for social media managers

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Adam Mosseri told Marina Mogilko, aka Silicon Valley Girl, that the artificial intelligence agent can help with ideation and trend discovery.

As Meta continues to expand access to its Muse artificial intelligence agents, which were made available to Australian users last week, social media managers may be wondering how they can use the tool within their process.

Instagram creator Marina Mogilko, who goes by the handle “Silicon Valley Girl,” recently interviewed Instagram Chief Adam Mosseri to get his insights on how creators and social media managers can use Meta’s AI agent to grow Instagram reach.

Mosseri said that Muse is good for ideation and coming up with resonant content concepts.

As per Mosseri: “If you’re trying to come up with more ideas, telling [Muse] what your goal is, then asking it for 10, 20, 30, 50 ideas, telling Muse which ones you like and which you don’t and iterating, it’s a great way just to get, sometimes, the creative juices going.”

Mosseri added that Muse can be helpful for evaluating content performance, and can assess what’s worked and what hasn’t in posts. He said the AI agent can also help categorize content.

Finally, Mosseri said Muse can be helpful for understanding trends.

“So for your audience, or for your industry, what are the trends that are happening right now on social media, not even just on Instagram,”Mosseri said. “Because that might surface conversations that you might want to jump in, for instance.”

Mogilko also asked Mosseri about Muse’s capacity to analyze followers, and provide assessment on the most influential followers in any sector. Mosseri said that Muse can provide a level of assessment of a profile’s audience, but Instagram is working on making this more valuable and effective.

Also interesting: Last month, Meta ran an ad for Muse which promoted the fact that the agent can alert Instagram users to people who have unfollowed them. Though as reported by Business Insider, it quickly took down the promotion after realizing that it goes against Instagram’s ethos.

Wired also reported that some people have been using Muse to unfollow accounts that don’t follow them back.

The latter two use cases are probably not what Meta wants to promote, but they do provide additional considerations for how the agent could be used to assist in automating some aspects of digital marketing.

#7373. Chief Customer Officer at Xapo Bank

Diversity is at the heart of who we are at Xapo Bank. We’re a fully distributed team of over 160 Xapiens that work remotely from 50+ countries around the world.

Our beginning: A world that enjoys economic freedom and wealth protection,no matter where you live or who is running your country.To achieve that, we search the world for the best people for the job. We work hard, think globally, and inspire each other to learn and grow. We are committed to changing the way things are done.

Although we are headquartered in Gibraltar, this is a full time, 100% remote position Work from anywhere!

Xapo's product suite has grown from a Bitcoin vault into a full member proposition: BTC and USD accounts that pay interest, a global card with Bitcoin cashback, Bitcoin-backed loans, a growing suite of BTC wealth and credit products, and access to stocks, ETFs, and stablecoins, all inside one regulated relationship.

Xapo is a bank, and a bank earns on the money its members choose to hold with it. Each of those products shipped well. What hasn't yet existed is a single owner of the economics of the customer relationship: one person accountable for winning the right members, growing what they hold with us, and keeping them, and for the balance-sheet products that make that possible.

The Chief Customer Officer is a new role at the top of the house, reporting to the CEO. You will run the stream that grows what members hold with Xapo, and you will own the Customer P&L, retail and institutional. It brings growth, client coverage, product management, and product design under one leader who is judged on customer contribution, the assets attracted and kept, and the members who stay. This is a customer-focused role in the most commercial sense: what a member earns from us, not the feature we shipped, is the centre of every decision.

The measure of success is a Customer P&L that grows on what members hold and keep: LTV:CAC improving, approved-to-paid rising, churn falling, and customer contribution the business can plan against.

This is a banking role, not a requirements-gathering role, a marketing role, or a role you can run from a dashboard. Products are priced on the balance sheet and judged on the money they attract and keep.

This part matters as much as the mandate. The known failure mode for this role, in any company, is a CCO with a polished customer-insight deck and no ownership of the number. That is disqualifying here.

Day 30: The Customer P&L baseline is documented across retail and institutional: customer contribution, LTV:CAC, approved-to-paid, churn, net paid-member growth, and assets attracted and kept. You have formed your own independent view of where members are won, lost, and under-served, and shared it with the CEO and Board.Day 60: The unified Customer operating model is live: one set of key results across Growth, Client Coverage, Mission PMs, and Product Design, read weekly from one source. Every mission PM owns a product's contribution and its price, and the roadmap is ranked on what it earns, built with Finance and the line leads.Day 90: At least one measurable improvement in LTV:CAC, approved-to-paid, churn, or net new AUM flow is live and attributable to a change you made, not a feature ship, an outcome moved. Every cell in your line has defined key results and an owner who explains the number every week.

#7372. How SharkNinja is doubling down on its creator strategy

The home appliance brand introduced two new creator programs, SharkNinja First Fans and SharkNinja Storytellers, to tap into the quickly growing influencer economy.

SharkNinja CEO Mark Barrocas in 2008 told a retailer that his plan was to build the company “one five-star review at a time.” In Barrocas’ retelling, the retailer’s executives dismissed the idea as foolish because they couldn’t imagine who would write a review of the brand’s products. That was before the rise of influencers.

Over the ensuing 28 years, SharkNinja has become a multibillion-dollar global company, which built its brand through a social-forward, ultra-connected strategy that includes partnerships with celebrities including David Beckham, Courteney Cox and Alix Earle, alongside a host of influencers.

SharkNinja is doubling down on that strategy with two new programs designed to give storytellers, both inside and outside of the company, access and opportunities to develop and create even more content.

The programs, SharkNinja First Fans, for company employees, and SharkNinja Storytellers, for general consumers and creators, are designed to help the company continue to grow and manage its expanding list of creators and partners.

“We felt we were underserving this community by not creating a space where we could have more scaled one-to-ones with them, bring them further into the fold in terms of our product board maps, and incentivize participation,” said Michelle Crossan-Matos, chief brand and experience officer at SharkNinja.

Over 200,000 posts about SharkNinja’s varied household products, which include blenders, vacuums and ice-cream makers, have been made this year, garnering more than 19 billion impressions, according to the company. Last year, it recorded more than $6.4 billion in sales.

The secret sauce is the company’s practice of fostering, nurturing and actively supporting those who want to create content around SharkNinja’s products, according to Crossan-Matos.

“We bring creators all the way upstream with our products, and we’re having them react to and test and make content with some of our products before we go to market. It’s always been core for our strategy,” said Crossan-Matos.

The new programs use leaderboards and rewards to ensure the content keeps coming. For outside creators, the rewards, which can include commissions and perks, are tied to growth and activity. The most active creators will get exclusive first looks at upcoming products and even get a voice in shaping them. The company has created tutorials and other materials, including an artificial intelligence-powered app, to help the internal creators develop compelling narratives.

Though not exactly commonplace, employer-supported creator programs are not unheard of either. Starbucks has its Green Apron Creators, IBM has a Buzz Squad, Gap opened up its creator ecosystem to employees, and Dell has compensated its employees for sharing content on their own channels. The scope of SharkNinja’s creator efforts are notable.

“I don't know if anybody is doing it the exact way that we are,” Crossan-Matos said. “I think to have both [consumer and employee programs] launch as quickly as we did and at this scale … Our appetite is to drive this globally.”

The company can support these programs on a global scale because of its broad product base, Crossan-Matos said. SharkNinja creates products across 41 consumer categories and launches an average of 25 new products every year.

“We're very lucky to have so many products for so many different types of communities globally,” Crossan-Matos said. “Creators just fit so seamlessly into our co-creation and our storytelling. We think [these initiatives] are going to propel more people to tell their own stories in a way that is even more relatable because they're everyday people.”

Keeping an eye on metrics will be key to measuring program success.

“We’ll be looking at content performance, just like we do with everything. We will be looking for what posts are going viral, what things are gaining traction,” Crossan-Matos said. “We expect really high numbers as we expand.”

#7371. X adds new video thumbnail and caption options

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The platform continues to build out its video tools in hopes of encouraging more uploads from users.

X added some new video creation tools on Friday, as the platform keeps pushing for more uploads in order to drive in-app engagement.

First, X reiterated that video is the fastest-growing format in the app.

As per X: “Posts with video get 5x the reach and engagement, and 36% of all impressions now go to video.”

X has been leaning into video content since 2024, when it reported that 4 out of 5 user sessions in the app included video consumption, and overall video views were growing at a rate of 35% year-over-year.

Given these stats, it makes sense for X to keep adding video updates, and for creators to pay attention in order to tap into the expanded reach potential of video clips.

X’s latest video features include improved captions, the capability to choose a video thumbnail, and more layout options.

On captions, X said creators now have more styles and color to choose from, providing another creative consideration.

Captions have been a big focus of X's video push, increasing the accessibility and viewability of videos in-stream.

X added multi-language captions, as translated by Grok in July, while it also rolled out an updated captioning process in October, which includes the option to manually edit captions in the composer, or ask Grok to correct them.

These latest additions will make captions a more dynamic option within X’s video toolkit.

Creators can also now manually choose a video thumbnail frame from their uploaded clip.

That could help creators ensure that their videos stand out in-stream.

Indeed, the right cover image can be a big lure in driving more video engagement. That’s why YouTube’s top creator MrBeast reportedly pays up to $10,000 per thumbnail for his clips, and generates up to 20 variations for consideration with each upload.

Another potentially valuable consideration for creators.

X also added more text overlay tools, as well as new layout options to help format video clips.

As explained by X: “Short videos play best vertical. They fill the whole screen, so viewers stay locked in. Now you can turn a horizontal video into a vertical one in one tap with Fill, Fade, or Stack. Just tap Edit when you upload.”

The new features build on X’s other recent video additions, including a fully revised video creation flow. X is also working to ensure that in-stream videos load faster, while the app has also launched new incentive programs for video creators, and new tools for live-streaming.

Given the engagement stats, this focus makes sense, and it could be worth experimenting with video clips on X to see how they perform in the app.

#7369. Bumble cozies up to Alix Earle in attempt to convert Gen Zers

The influencer, who has previously stated her dislike of dating apps, appears in a two-minute video alongside Pete Davidson to encourage Gen Z users to give the platform a try.

Bumble is looking to appeal to Gen Z users as the demographic continues to ditch apps for real-life alternatives. User retention continues to be a problem for the dating app, which saw the total number of paying users decline from 2.5 million in Q2 2025 to 2.1 million in Q2 2026, according to an earnings statement.

The casting choices for the campaign are interesting ones as Earle has routinely rejected dating apps and Davidson is known for his string of ill-fated relationships with high-profile individuals, including a short-lived engagement to pop star Ariana Grande.

The video is self-aware regarding the history of its stars. For example, when Davidson plays an inconsiderate first date, Earle asks what Davidson does for work. He responds "Nothing much. I just kind of talk to camera.” Earle responds that she does something similar, to which Davidson replies, “yeah, but when I do it, it’s different,” a reference to controversial comments the comedian made regarding large influencer salaries and the amount of work involved.

Earle’s character is similarly aware of her past with dating apps. When confronted with the fact that she has publicly stated she hates dating apps, she responds: “I have said that publicly at least five different times on three different platforms. But sometimes I can be a little dramatic.”

Over the course of the sexual innuendo-laden spot, Earle convinces her fellow Gen Zers to try Bumble, showing off features such as searching for specific people. The women are impressed by the quality of men they find on the site, with one participant being impressed they all have bedframes.

The campaign was created in partnership with OBB Bolded and is supported by Bumble data that found 81% of singles between the ages of 18 and 25 are most interested in a relationship that adds value to the life they’re building.

Bumble has worked to attract more users to its app in recent months, including allowing anyone in a match to send the first message, a deviation away from the previous model where women had to send the first message, which was once a selling point for the brand. It also expanded the response window from 24 to 72 hours and introduced handles, a tool that allows verified users to more easily find one another on the app.

This isn’t the first time Bumble has turned to influencer marketing. In June, the app launched “Bee Line,” a talk show hosted by comedian and influencer Jake Shane that tackles dating anxiety.

#7368. Pinterest announces partnership with Microsoft Ads

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The new integration will see Pinterest ad placements extended across Microsoft’s partner platforms.

Pinterest has announced a new integration with Microsoft Advertising, which will make Pinterest ad placements available to Microsoft platform users.

Microsoft Ads is primarily focused on placements within Microsoft’s own ecosystem, but it also incorporates a range of partner sites and platforms, enabling advertisers to expand their promotions. And now, Pinterest will be added to that list of partner platforms.

As explained by Pinterest: “Microsoft Advertising customers’ campaigns will have access to Pinterest’s visual search environment through a custom contextual bidding model. Eligible Microsoft Advertising campaigns can access Pinterest's open-auction inventory across home feed, search, and related Pins, expanding opportunities to engage consumers throughout their discovery journeys.”

Pinterest added that targeting for its Microsoft Ads integration will be built on Pinterest search queries, contextual signals, and first-party intent data.

“[T]he model identifies relevant ad placements across Pinterest’s visual search adjacent inventory,” Pinterest said. “The integration uses Pinterest Intelligence, Pinterest’s AI-powered understanding of people’s interests, combining hundreds of billions of connections with visual-understanding technology and behavioral signals to surface personalized interests and anticipate what users may want next.”

Pinterest has been working to expand its ad business in order to boost its revenue potential. Pinterest's ad intake has been growing, but its third quarter revenue intake fell short of Wall Street expectations, while it's also encountered regulatory restrictions in the EU market.

Last month, Pinterest announced a new partnership with Magnite that will make Pinterest’s ad inventory available via multiple ad exchanges, including Yahoo DSP and Amazon Ads DVA+, as well as Google Display and Video 360.

The new partnership with Microsoft will feed even more ads into Pinterest’s system.

Pinterest said its ad inventory will initially be available via Microsoft Ads in North America, Australia and New Zealand.

#7365. Pinterest simplifies parental controls

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The platform has updated its parental control dashboard to offer a more streamlined way to manage devices and access options.

Pinterest has updated its parental control elements to offer a more integrated, streamlined process and make it easier for parents to manage their child’s in-app experience.

As shown in these example screens, Pinterest’s updated parental controls dashboard now includes all of the app’s oversight and management options in one place, including profile visibility, content recommendations and connection controls.

The updated parental controls also include direct links to manage device-level screen time and location settings. Parents will also be able to make their kids’ profiles private by default and set limits on ad personalization and social features.

In addition, Pinterest added tools that allow parents to control the amount of artificial intelligence-generated content that teens see in the app. There’s also new notification management functionality.

Parents can also decide whether their teens have autoplay video switched on or not, which could help to combat compulsive viewing behaviors.

Pinterest CEO Bill Ready said the platform is focused on building an experience that’s age-appropriate for teens from the start, with protections that are built in, “not bolted on.”

“For parents who want more involvement, the controls are easy to find and simple to use,” Ready said. “Families can choose the experience that is right for them, while teens can continue to explore their interests and feel inspired.”

Pinterest has been working to present its app as an alternative to potentially harmful, engagement-focused approaches that have been adopted by other social media platforms.

In September, Pinterest published a report on how teens use the app, which showed that more than 77% of its teen audience uses Pinterest to explore creative interests.

More teen control options will provide additional peace of mind for parents, which could help to further establish Pinterest as a safer space for young users.

“Sociable” is the latest commentary on important social media developments and trends from industry expert Andrew Hutchinson of Social Media Today.

Instagram has added another way for creators to make money, by partnering with Amazon to enable affiliate links for Amazon-listed products in Reels and feed posts.

As shown in these example images, creators can select from a range of products on Amazon to add to their posts. Clickable links to the relevant product listings on Amazon will then be added in the bottom left of a post or Reel display, allowing viewers to easily make a purchase.

All affiliate links will be connected to the creator’s account, and creators will earn a commission for any sales generated from those referrals.

Eligible creators can link their Instagram and Amazon Influencer accounts in their Professional Dashboard on IG in order to facilitate product linking.

As per an Instagram press release sent to SMT: “Once connected, Instagram automatically includes their affiliate links when they add Amazon products to content, with product links taking viewers directly to the Amazon Shopping App.”

Instagram also said creators will be able to add up to 30 products per Reel, or 20 per feed post. This should provide a heap of linking potential for affiliate opportunities.

Creators can also see the commission rate for each item, so they’ll know how much they’ll get from any resulting link clicks.

This is another way for Instagram to provide monetization pathways for its creators, while also giving Amazon another means to promote its products via creator endorsement.

Amazon has been steadily expanding its product display opportunities, with the shopping giant also inking similar affiliate partnerships with YouTube and Pinterest this year.

Though, interestingly, Amazon asked to be removed from the list of platforms that will work with Meta’s Muse agent Amazon said that was because the Muse system was in violation of Amazon’s automated shopping tool restrictions.

A partnership with Instagram, then, seems like an interesting development, which could also lead to Amazon eventually working with Meta’s other platforms more openly.

#7359. Walmart mulls role advertising will play in an agentic shopping world

Momentum for the retailer’s ad business remained strong in Q3, strengthened by assets like Vizio and an expansion of its e-commerce marketplace.

Walmart’s U.S. advertising revenue grew 37% year over year in the three-month period ended Oct. 31, bolstered by strengths in e-commerce and assets like Vizio and Vibe.co. Walmart Connect, which makes up the lion’s share of Walmart’s U.S. ad segment, was up 36% in Q3, excluding the impact of Vizio and Vibe.co, according to an earnings statement.

Vizio sold TV hardware at a steady clip, with unit volume up nearly 150% YoY, which broadens the audience Walmart advertisers can reach through the platform’s operating system, Chief Growth Officer Seth Dallaire said. The Vizio and Vibe.co acquisitions are part of Walmart’s strategy to shore up a foothold in connected TV, a premium video channel that diversifies its retail media footprint beyond onsite formats like sponsored search and display. Vibe.co, a self-service TV advertising platform, was recently integrated into Vizio and Walmart’s larger CTV offering following the acquisition’s close in August.

“We're now able to deliver capability for sales attribution through those Vizio television sets in ways that we have never been able to do before,” Dallaire said of the deal on a call discussing the retailer’s fiscal 2027 Q3. “We have a lot of room to run as we continue to sell more TVs.”

E-commerce grew 23% in Q3, with the addition of new merchants to Walmart’s online marketplace providing tailwinds for Connect. Stripping out advertising, Walmart’s e-commerce business is close to breaking even, CFO John Rainey said on the earnings call. Walmart raised its outlook for the year around the report, expecting sales growth between 4.9% to 5.2% compared to a prior forecast of 4% to 5% growth.

Executives were asked about the impact agentic artificial intelligence could have on retail media. Consumer-facing agents like Meta’s Muse can seek out deals, make product comparisons and complete transactions on the user’s behalf, which disintermediates the role ads typically play on the shopping journey.

Consumer curiosity about new products and brands hasn’t changed even as AI alters how they explore their options, per Dallaire, who nodded to the potential for Walmart to experiment with advertising in an agentic world. Walmart has its own conversational assistant, Sparky, which has seen usage in the U.S. grow 129% this year, the retailer reported. Sparky launched in June 2025.

“Conversational commerce and the way that people are creating queries and prompts in these agents is quite different than what we have seen historically,” said Dallaire. “But we are learning about those prompts and how to serve customers and allow marketers and brands to get their products in front of customers.”

Walmart is looking at agentic capabilities through two lenses as it relates to Vizio and Vibe.Co, Dallaire explained in response to an analyst follow-up question. One is the consumer-facing element, such as evolving how content is discovered and served via Vizio. Vibe.Co meanwhile is using agentic technology on the back end to draw in more small- and medium-sized advertisers that don’t have the budgets for high gloss TV campaigns.

#7355. Coca-Cola pivots from divisive AI-generated ads for holiday campaign

“Enjoy Joy” spots are part of a seasonal push that includes digital and social content, experiential activations and packaging.

Coca-Cola is going back to basics with the recently launched “Enjoy Joy” spots, showcasing moments of connection and togetherness in a decidedly traditional way. The creative direction comes after the brand ran ads during the last two years made with generative AI that — despite exceeding internal benchmarks — proved divisive with consumers. The new ads were directed by Paul Dektor and produced by Mayan Productions and arrive as holiday marketers double down on human-made creative.

The “Enjoy Joy” spots, including versions tailored to the Hispanic market, are joined by a handful of extensions across channels. Coca-Cola will run creator-led content across Meta, TikTok, Pinterest and YouTube, along with a “Grandma's Holiday Table” social series that focuses on the “abuelas, nonnas, nanas, aunties and tías” who bring holiday traditions to life. The campaign will also span streaming, audio, cinema and out-of-home channels and includes an Amazon media partnership featuring creator and commerce integrations.

“There's something special about the role Coca‑Cola plays during the holidays. People look forward to seeing how we'll show up each year, whether it's through the traditions they know and love or something entirely unexpected,” said Stacy Jackson, vice president for the Coca‑Cola Trademark, in a statement. “It's about finding new ways to make Coca‑Cola part of the season while staying true to what people have always loved about the brand.”

The brand’s long-running holiday caravan tour kicked off Nov. 5 in Nashville and will make more than 270 stops nationwide, including New York City's Times Square on Nov. 24. Each stop includes activities like photos with Santa Claus and Coke’s polar bear mascot, a gifting cabin and a beverage station. The caravan also ties into the brand’s partnership with the USO, giving consumers an opportunity to share messages with those who serve in the military.

During the holiday season, Coca‑Cola, Coca‑Cola Zero Sugar and Diet Coke will offer limited-edition packaging featuring Santa Claus, who also makes a brief appearance in the ad creative. Coca‑Cola Holiday Creamy Vanilla and its zero-sugar variant will also return to shelves for a limited time.

Coca-Cola grew net revenues by 7% to $13.4 billion in Q3 2026, beating Wall Street estimates.. The earnings were released days after the company announced the completion of its global marketing operating system review, selecting Omnicom as its media partner in North America. WPP Open X will continue to serve as Coca-Cola’s global creative partner, while Omnicom will unite media, data, CRM, loyalty and creators in a connected ecosystem in North America. The new structure will be implemented in phases beginning Dec. 1.

#7352. Campaign Trail: Tiffany tells human holiday story with Hollywood talent

The luxury brand and agency American Haiku leaned into real emotions with actor Amanda Seyfried and director Derek Cianfrance.

In adland, it has been a decidedly handmade holiday season, with brands including Levi’s and E.l.f. turning to techniques like stop-motion animation to connect with consumers who are growing weary of ads created by artificial intelligence.

For its annual holiday effort, Tiffany & Co. found the best way to resonate with consumers is through human storytelling. The luxury brand’s global campaign, “Love is a Gift,” was created with agency American Haiku and revolves around a two-minute film starring actor Amanda Seyfried and director Derek Cianfrance.

The short, “You & Me,” jumps from the present day to New York City in the 1990s to tell the story of a young girl and her mother, played by Seyfried. The girl watches her mother work as a choreographer and has a handful of holiday experiences before being gifted with a Tiffany ornament that she shares with her own daughter in the present.

“Moving between past and present, the film reflects the enduring place Tiffany & Co. holds in life’s most meaningful moments and the stories we carry forward,” said CMO Andrea Davey in a statement.

The film is soundtracked by a cover of The Wannadies’ “You & Me Song,” a tune best known for its appearance on the 1996 “Romeo + Juliet” soundtrack. The campaign will run across cinema, paid and organic social, digital out-of-home, owned channels and clienteling across global channels.

Along with being on-trend with regard to stories imbued with humanity, Tiffany’s holiday campaign also represents a pivot from the brand’s past holiday creative. The 2025 edition of the “Love is a Gift” campaign turned its iconic blue boxes into portals to love stories around the world. This year, Tiffany brought on American Haiku, which had worked on a previous campaign for the brand in the U.K., but didn’t offer a traditional brief.

“They came to us with an initial idea of a family spending the holidays in their home and [tapping] into the memory aspect,” said Ben Muckensturm, creative director at the shop. “Where we pushed the work was bringing in the importance of the mother-daughter relationship that I think is the core of the story.”

Keying into the mother-daughter story gave the brand and agency a larger insight around the memory of seeing a parent as a person in their own world that is relatable to consumers, whether or not they are wealthy residents of the Upper East Side like the characters in the film. In the film, the true gift is not the ornament but the memory that is associated with it.

“That opened us up to how we explore the past and then bring it back to the present and create a piece that feels essentially real, that anyone could connect with,” Muckensturm said. “Everything was shot in New York. It was definitely an intentional push to try to bring it to the real world and make it more of an emotional piece.”

“You & Me” also delivers nostalgia for a pre-digital ‘90s that has been a reliable way to engage millennial audiences. However, the nostalgia in the film is not the traditional touchstones, like technology and boy bands, used by marketers looking to tap into memories of the decade. Instead, Tiffany looked at its own archives and at the holidays of movies like “Home Alone” and “The Parent Trap” for inspiration.

“When we created the town house, we went back to old archival Tiffany imagery of how things were,” Muckensturm said of creating the main set for the ad. “Especially on Fifth Avenue, most of the references that we brought were from ‘Home Alone 2,’ like what the streets looked like at the time. It's great to be able to tap into things that people are familiar with.”

After creating the world of the ad, the agency populated it with brand ambassador Seyfried, whose character is the mother in the past, rather than the main character in the present-day framing device. The actor, an Academy Award nominee whose performance in one of the year’s biggest films has captivated audiences, brought her gifts to the production.

“She has such a maternal instinct that really played perfectly on set, and you could see really how she was a mother to that girl for the days that we shot,” Muckensturm said.

The choice of Cianfrance, a director best known for dramatic fare like “Blue Valentine” and “The Place Beyond the Pines,” helped the brand and agency get the emotional tone right, without rehearsal and without falling into familiar or even corny holiday tropes.

“There was a trusting relationship between production partners, us and the client to come into it with a really open mind to see what the scene gives us,” Muckensturm said. “We knew where we were going to shoot, and we were trying to get a range of emotion… but we really let him direct them and let this play naturally.”

#7349. How Jell-O’s new creative platform looks to shift consumer perceptions

The campaign, the first by Johannes Leonardo for the Kraft Heinz brand, represents its largest marketing investment in more than a decade.

Jell-O on Monday launched a new creative platform, “Oh Hello, Jell-O,” that seeks to shift consumer perceptions about how the product can be enjoyed beyond traditional use cases. The effort represents the Kraft Heinz brand’s largest marketing investment in more than a decade, per details shared with Marketing Dive.

“As a nearly 130-year-old brand, we recognized a disconnect between how familiar consumers are with Jell-O and how often they think to purchase it,” Kathryn O’Brien, head of marketing for desserts at Kraft Heinz, said in emailed comments. “We want Jell-O to be more than something that comes to mind for a bowl of gelatin or pudding, but rather a part of the creative process in the kitchen.”

Central to the campaign are two 15-second spots that show home cooks in monochrome kitchens preparing desserts with Jell-O before a social-inspired flip transition pivots the scene to others marveling over the finished product.

The campaign was created by Johannes Leonardo and is the first campaign for the brand by the agency, which has held creative duties on select Kraft Heinz brands since 2020. The spots were directed by Drew Kirsch, a veteran of music videos who has worked with Taylor Swift, and feature an original electronic-pop song that uses “oh hello, Jell-O” as a vocal hook.

“Rather than borrowing an existing song, we saw an opportunity to build an ownable sonic identity around the platform,” O’Brien said. “The original track is a recognizable brand asset that can extend across social, content and future campaign moments.”

As part of the launch, Jell-O will take over the Las Vegas Sphere this week, transforming the orb into a gelatin mold, a “dirt cup” dessert and banana cream pudding. “Oh Hello, Jell-O” will run across streaming, online video, social and digital throughout 2027, with investment pulsing around key seasonal moments. The significant media investment comes at a pivotal moment for the brand, O’Brien explained.

“Our first-ever CTV buy allows us to bring the campaign's highly visual, music-driven creative to life on the big screen, showcasing the playfulness, vibrant colors and unexpected transformations in a high-attention environment,” the executive said. “We're taking an integrated approach throughout 2027, combining streaming and online video with social, digital and e-commerce touchpoints.”

The creative platform builds on a 2023 rebrand, crafted with agency Brand Opus, that updated Jell-O’s visual identity with a more modern look and feel. The rebrand, which at the time was its first such effort in 10 years, arrived amid an industry-wide move to help CPG brands engage with new consumer groups.

Kraft Heinz in February stopped plans to split its condiment and grocery staples businesses, with CEO Steve Cahillane saying many of the CPG company’s challenges are fixable. The company is pouring $700 million into a turnaround strategy that includes significant investments in marketing, which has been increased to at least 6% of net sales.

While Kraft Heinz saw organic net sales decrease 1.1% in Q3 2026, the company’s market share, sales and volume trends improved in every region, per an earnings report. Jell-O was cited on an earnings call as a brand with which the company is looking to win share by investing selectively.

#7347. Why more brands are paying creators to make their ads

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

This article is part of an ongoing series detailing the most important information readers need to know about the ad industry’s most complex topics. More from the series →

Brands paying influencers to make campaign creative have become key drivers of investment in the booming creator economy. Creative agencies might want to take note.

“You get the authentic, scroll-stopping content that people want to engage each with. But you also get the reach,” said Katy Ball, head of social at M&C Saatchi Sport & Entertainment.

As spending on paid social channels — and video in particular — continues to rise, demand for creative assets to appear in those ad slots is increasing.

The number of assets attached to individual campaigns has risen 30% in the last five years, according to a CreativeX study of 115,990 ad campaigns, representing $11 billion in ad spend. Per the study, just five assets receive 88% of media investment in an average campaign.

The need for more campaign assets is fueling the growth of asset-led spending, the fastest growing segment of the creator economy, according to a report published this week by research consultancy Madison & Wall.

Currently, 12% of the $112 billion spent on creators globally goes towards creators producing ads on behalf of brands, per the study. That’s expected to rise 16% every year through 2030.

The days when brands principally paid creators to rent their following are rapidly disappearing. Influencers are now media partners, ambassadors and increasingly, cogs in the creative production supply chain. And brands see creator-made ads as a solution to their social asset shortage.

“For us, the appeal is simple. Buying space in someone’s feed doesn’t mean you’ve earned their attention. Good creators understand what their audiences care about and how to give them something worth stopping for,” said Jared Kozel, co-founder and chief creative officer at agency Super Nice. “That’s valuable creative judgment to bring into an ad no matter the brand or category.”

Influencer marketing experts note that several different but related practices are included under the broader umbrella of creator-led production.

While some brands simply pay creators a fee in order to receive video or still assets for use in a campaign, whitelisting (also called “dark advertising”) has become a favored method of managing such arrangements.

In this context, an influencer grants a brand limited access to their social media accounts, allowing them to book a paid media campaign through that account, using assets made by the creator while taking advantage of discrete audience targeting.

“What we’re seeing is a lot of recutting of media spend to be allocated towards creator development in order to fund whitelisting,” said Olivia Wedderburn, head of influence at Born Social.

Madison & Wall’s research suggested that funding for creative production may also be coming from PR, social or experimental budgets, as well as traditional media or production pots of money.

Another related practice, user generated content, sees brands paying regular social media users to license their content as creative assets in ad campaigns.

“They have to feed their their content engines, and they’re opening up as many different avenues as they can,” said Andy Ryan, co-founder at social and influencer agency Komodo.

The relative low cost of working with influencers, versus creative production agencies, is the primary driver behind brand spending on creator-made assets.

Although production spending is often a small fraction of an overall campaign budget, marketers are keen to squeeze every non-working (that is, non-media) dollar for all it’s worth. While that same desire is pushing some brands toward generative AI production techniques, others are turning to creators.

But as this type of spending grows, so to does the need to manage it effectively. “It’s never been more complicated to negotiate usage rights or exclusivity,” said Wedderburn.

Billion Dollar Boy, for example, recently added features to its Companion creator management tool designed to better facilitate creator-led production efforts and manage usage rights negotiations.

“The creator economy has never been more competitive, heightening the urgency for brands to understand the market context,” said Thomas Walters, the agency’s chief innocation officer and co-founder.

At the same time, increased brand spending in this area is already leading to an uptick in the fees commanded by some creators. Last year, agency practitioners reported creator rates ticking up 10-20% due to demand for expanded rights.

There’s also some evidence to show that creator-made assets perform as well as, or even better than, traditional advertising spots in a social context.

A report by System1, WPP Media and Goat published in June found that creator ads achieved 3.2X the brand-awareness lift for category leader ads as traditional advertising creative.

“We’re seeing a lot of brands say that is more valuable in terms of conversion and reach than some of the quick-and-dirty assets they previously would have relied on,” said Wedderburn.

That’s not unexpected. Audiences recognize the visual cues, language and production methods employed by creators as native to TikTok or Instagram, while clocking films shot on a closed set or using more traditional methods as foreign that same environment, a lesson that major advertisers like Nike are reluctantly absorbing.

“If programs are set up correctly, creators can deliver volume and variety faster and more cost effectively than a traditional production cycle,” said Nicholas Spiro, chief commercial officer, Viral Nation. “The shift we’re seeing is brands starting to plan creators across their media budgets, rather than as a separate influencer line item alone.”

Walmart is allowing access to Meta’s Muse through a gateway that lets it control how AI agents browse, shop and make purchases.

Amazon is paying to reach ChatGPT shoppers while the chatbot is finding other ways to surface its products and deals.

Holiday marketing is changing: CTV/streaming and TV ads are gaining traction in 2026.

#7346. Philadelphia whips up bigger holiday marketing spend amid brand revamp

Brand character Phillyboy returns in a Santa-like role to dish out blocks of cream cheese to be used in cheesecake recipes.

“Really Philly Good,” which debuted in February, was developed to broaden consumer perceptions of what Philadelphia has to offer. Rather than only showing the product as a cold spread for bagels and snacks, the platform highlights how cream cheese can be used to enrich more involved meals. A larger marketing push around Q4 responds to the insight that one-third of Philadelphia cream cheese bricks are sold during the November-December period and Google search trends data that show spikes in interest for cheesecake recipes during the season.

In the new work, Phillyboy acts as a Santa-like figure, trotting into houses saddled on his dairy cow to dole out blocks of cream cheese that are then used to make cheesecake. The rugged Western-themed character is accompanied by a spin on Christmas standards like “Jingle Bells.” Agency Johannes Leonardo is behind “Really Philly Good” while Nalle Sjöblad, from Spark & Riot, directed the holiday ad spots. The full media plan spans TV, streaming, connected TV, online video, social, creators and retail elements.

Beyond video advertising, Philadelphia is running a national integration with “Happy Hour with Ina Garten” that is supported by sponsored social content and a custom cheesecake recipe on the Barefoot Contessa website and Substack. Other social and digital activations include a cheesecake-building experience on Pinterest, an augmented reality Snapchat lens and a focus on TikTok search and trending food and drink Reels content on Meta.

In addition, the Kraft Heinz marketer enlisted TikTok and Instagram creators, including Tineke “Tini” Younger and Kiley O’Donnell, for holiday cheesecake content. The creator program started on Nov. 2 and has so far drawn nearly 1 million organic views and 43,000 engagements, the brand said.

Kraft Heinz is broadly revamping its portfolio as it tries to win back consumers who have shifted toward protein-rich and better-for-you offerings. In August, it announced plans to spend an additional $100 million on its turnaround, with the lion’s share of the investment concentrated in marketing. Marketing will represent at least 6% of the company’s net sales this year.

Jell-O, another brand under Kraft Heinz, unveiled a new creative platform on Monday that is backed by its largest marketing investment in more than a decade. Johannes Leonardo also handled “Oh Hello, Jell-O,” the shop’s first work for the brand.

#7343. Carl’s Jr. taps David&Goliath as marketing focus turns to boldness

The agency of record appointment includes a mandate to lean into the QSR’s heritage and forward-looking initiatives like a Burger Revolution strategy.

Carl’s Jr. has appointed David&Goliath as marketing agency of record as it shifts focus to cooked-to-order burgers and tries to revive a bolder, boundary-pushing brand personality, according to news shared with Marketing Dive. Carl’s Jr. did not previously have a dedicated AOR, and instead worked with agencies on a project basis, Marketing Dive understands.

David&Goliath, which is part of Innocean Worldwide, will oversee brand strategy, creative development, experiential marketing, production and storytelling for the fast-food chain, with a mandate to lean into Carl’s Jr.'s heritage while shoring up cultural relevance with younger consumers. Its first work is expected to arrive in Q1 of next year.

CKE Restaurants Holdings-owned Carl’s Jr. unveiled its Burger Revolution strategy in September, which introduces a systemwide cooked-to-order approach to burger preparation. The announcement was accompanied by the release of a limited-time Angus Maximus 5.7-ounce burger. The changes are part of a larger effort by Carl’s Jr. to emphasize food quality, which has manifested in promotional areas like limited-time offerings.

Other fast-food companies, including rival Burger King, have thrown a spotlight on premium ingredients and restaurant improvements to win back price-sensitive diners. Carl’s Jr.’s franchised store count has declined in recent years. Franchisees of the brand and sister restaurant Hardee’s have faced their own profitability struggles, with a major one in Calirfornia in April declaring bankruptcy, Marketing Dive’s sister publication Restaurant Dive previously reported.

Carl’s Jr. has made internal changes to its marketing leadership this year as well. In the spring, CKE Restaurants named Burge Diemer, a restaurant industry vet who previously worked at brands including The Habit Burger & Grill, Boston Market and Jack in the Box, as CMO of Carl’s Jr. Diemer is tasked with developing breakthrough campaigns and driving product innovation. She credited David&Goliath with possessing the bravery necessary to build on Carl’s Jr.’s legacy.

“Together, we’re excited to push boundaries, expand our connection with customers, and bring the unmistakable Carl’s Jr. spirit to a new generation of burger lovers,” Diemer said in a press statement.

Carl’s Jr.’s advertising has not shied away from pushing buttons in the past. The chain in the 2000s became known for TV commercials featuring bikini-clad models suggestively eating burgers. It has dipped back into the racy well in recent years, including through a 2025 campaign with influencer Alix Earle that touted offerings like a hangover-themed burger.

#7342. Anthropic says no to ads but Wall Street may have other ideas

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Anthropic is a public company now, which puts it on an unofficial path to an ads business.

Unofficial because the company’s official position is still firmly against ads. It went as far as spending Super Bowl money on a campaign mocking OpenAI for bringing them to ChatGPT. Its prospectus, the document pitching those public shares to investors, leaves advertisers out of the business altogether.

“Is it cynical to expect Anthropic to follow the same route? Not really. More like an educated guess,” said ad tech expert Shirley Marschall.

Besides, the company has already left the door open, she continued. Its pledge rules out sponsored links adjacent to conversations, but in the same post it says it will keep building features that help users “find, compare, or buy products, connect with businesses.” And once an agent recommends products, retail media will pay to be in those recommendations, Marschall said, before adding: “Let’s see Anthropic turn that ad revenue down,” she added.

Advertisers, for their part, will be watching closely, and with mixed feelings. On the one hand, a new media seller means a new platform to wrangle and one more set of tools and teams to learn at a time when most are still working out how to buy ChatGPT. On the other hand, Claude’s audience is also spending more and more time in those conversation threads. For marketers, that’s a hard place to stay out of for long.

“Anthropic, like any company, has a stance towards handling consumer data and inadvertently how advertising is considered,” said independent ad tech consultant Jonathan D’Souza Rauto. “But monetization is a lucrative form of revenue. I’d expect Anthropic to have a change of heart. Look no further to how Apple has played this advertising game over the past few years despite being considered anti-advertising.”

Life as a public company isn’t cheap, after all, and it’s even less cheap for an AI company that has signed up for approximately $895.4 billion in compute and infrastructure commitments, some running to 2045. That’s more than 13 years of revenue at its current pace, given Q3 revenue of $17 billion. The revenue covering that bill is far less locked in since 80% of revenue is consumption-based and the S-1 says many customers can cut usage or terminate on short notice. In fact, the company has already warned that “operating margins may compress when large tranches arrive.”

Then there’s the free tier. “Free and promotional users may never convert to paid plans,” the filing admits, yet Anthropic still pays to serve every one of them. Analysts found that cost sits in sales and marketing out of sight of the headline margin. That arrangement holds as long as free users keep upgrading. If they stop, Anthropic is left with a growing audience it pays to serve and earns nothing from.

OpenAI has already shown what that audience could be worth. ChatGPT ads reached a $1 billion annualized revenue run rate less than 200 days after launching. When both companies are trading, analysts will ask Anthropic why it’s leaving money on the table.

“They’ll go after advertising, just not in the way some assume,” said Rob Webster, founder and CEO of TAU Marketing Solutions. “The prize for Anthropic isn’t ads inside Claude. Advertising is now a trillion-dollar market, and the real power sits with whatever brain coordinates it: deciding what runs, where, and why. That’s a far more valuable position than selling impressions. Anthropic wants to be a new, better Microsoft or Apple. Selling tools to businesses. Not ad opportunities.”

There are reasons, though, why Anthropic may resist the lure of ads for as long as it feasibly can.

“Trust and impartiality really matter with LLMs, particularly among enterprise customers,” said Alex Tait, founder of Entropy. “In contrast to OpenAI, Anthropic is currently approaching operating break-even without ads suggesting its existing business model could be commercially sustainable without it.”

Anthropic’s anti-ads stance is based on its perspective that once ads become part of a business’s revenue targets, the pressure to maximize engagement can start influencing product decisions. For an AI app, in this case Claude, that creates a conflict: users expect Claude to help them make decisions in their own interests, not towards whatever generates revenue for the company or its advertisers. And in its IPO prospectus, the company said that they want “Claude’s only incentive to be giving them [users] a helpful answer,” which is why they have “chosen not to introduce that pressure [ads] into Claude.”

Anthropic did not respond to Digiday’s request for comment.
